title: The Agent Loop From Scratch
summary: An agent is a loop, not a library. This topic builds a full reason → act → observe loop by hand: raw calls to a provider-agnostic client, a tool registry that maps names to Python functions, a growing message list that accumulates every step, and an explicit stop condition. Once you can write the loop from scratch, every framework you meet later is just sugar over these same four moving parts.

subtopics.title: The loop is three repeating phases
subtopics.explanation: Every agent step does the same three things: the model reasons about the next action, your code acts by running the requested tool, and you observe by appending the result back into the conversation. You repeat until the model stops asking for tools. Getting these three phases explicit in your own code is what demystifies every agent framework you will ever touch.
subtopics.example:
# one turn of the loop, spelled out
resp = client.chat(messages, tools=TOOLS)      # 1. reason
if not resp.tool_calls:                         # model is done
    return resp.content
for call in resp.tool_calls:                     # 2. act
    result = REGISTRY[call.name](**call.args)
    messages.append(tool_result(call.id, result))  # 3. observe
# ...then loop again with the enriched messages

subtopics.title: A tool registry maps names to functions
subtopics.explanation: The model can only emit a tool *name* and arguments as text; it cannot reach your functions. A registry — a plain dict from name to callable — is the lookup table your code uses to turn that name into a real function call. Keeping the registry separate from the loop means adding a new capability is just registering one more function.

subtopics.title: Messages accumulate the whole trajectory
subtopics.explanation: There is no hidden state — the agent's entire memory is the list of messages you carry from turn to turn. Each turn you append the model's request and the tool's result, so the next call sees everything that happened. The message list growing over time is literally the agent thinking out loud on paper.
subtopics.example:
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": goal}]
# after the model asks for a tool, append BOTH sides:
messages.append({"role": "assistant", "tool_calls": resp.tool_calls})
messages.append({
    "role": "tool",
    "tool_call_id": call.id,
    "content": str(result),   # the observation
})
# every later client.chat(messages) now 'remembers' this step

subtopics.title: Talk to the provider with raw calls
subtopics.explanation: Under any framework, an agent is just repeated HTTP-style calls to a chat endpoint, passing the messages and the tool schemas and reading back either content or tool calls. We use a provider-agnostic pseudo-client so the shape is clear: `client.chat(messages, tools)` returns an object with `.content` and `.tool_calls`. Seeing the raw request/response shape is what lets you debug any provider or swap between them.
subtopics.example:
# provider-agnostic shape used throughout this topic
resp = client.chat(
    messages=messages,      # full running history
    tools=TOOL_SCHEMAS,     # JSON Schemas the model may call
    temperature=0,
)
# resp.content     -> final text, or None if it wants a tool
# resp.tool_calls  -> list of {id, name, args} or empty
if resp.tool_calls:
    handle(resp.tool_calls)

subtopics.title: A stop condition ends the loop
subtopics.explanation: Because the model chooses its own next step, the loop needs an explicit exit or it can run forever and burn budget. The natural signal is 'the model returned content and no tool calls', but you also add a hard step cap as a backstop. Combining a natural done-signal with a hard cap is what turns an open-ended loop into a bounded, production-safe one.
subtopics.example:
MAX_STEPS = 8
for step in range(MAX_STEPS):
    resp = client.chat(messages, tools=TOOL_SCHEMAS)
    if not resp.tool_calls:        # natural stop: model answered
        return resp.content
    run_tools(resp.tool_calls)     # keep going
raise RuntimeError("agent hit step cap without finishing")

foundations.overview: An agent is a large language model placed inside a control loop that you own. Each iteration has three phases: reason (call the model with the running conversation and the available tool schemas), act (execute whichever tool the model requested using a registry that maps tool names to Python functions), and observe (append the tool's result back into the message list so the next call sees it). The message list is the agent's only memory — there is no hidden state — so it grows monotonically as the trajectory unfolds. The loop terminates on a natural signal (the model returns final content with no tool calls) guarded by a hard step cap so it can never run forever. We deliberately use a provider-agnostic pseudo-client with a `chat(messages, tools)` method returning `.content` and `.tool_calls`, because every real provider is a variation on this same shape. Writing all four pieces — raw call, registry, message accumulation, stop condition — by hand is the single best way to understand what frameworks like LangChain or the SDKs are actually doing under the hood.
foundations.formalDefinition: The agent loop is an iterative procedure: given a message history H and tool schemas T, repeatedly (1) compute response R = model(H, T); (2) if R has no tool calls, return R.content; (3) otherwise, for each tool call c in R, execute registry[c.name](**c.args), append the assistant tool-call message and a tool-result message keyed by c.id to H; (4) repeat until step 2 fires or a maximum iteration count is exceeded.
foundations.whyItMatters: Frameworks hide the loop, but the loop is where every real bug lives: an unterminated loop, a mismatched tool-call id, a tool result never fed back, a missing step cap. Engineers who have written the loop from scratch can read any agent stack, debug it fast, and build a minimal one when a heavy framework is overkill. It is the literacy that everything else in agent engineering builds on.
foundations.mentalModel: Picture a dispatcher (your loop) sitting between a brilliant analyst who can only pass notes (the model) and a bank of machines (your tools). The analyst writes 'run get_weather(Paris)' on a note; the dispatcher finds that machine in the directory (the registry), runs it, staples the printout to the growing case file (the messages), and hands the whole file back. This repeats until the analyst writes a final answer instead of another machine request.
foundations.realWorldUsage: This exact loop underlies coding assistants that read files and run tests, research agents that search and summarize, support agents that look up orders and issue refunds, and data agents that query warehouses. Production stacks wrap it with retries, logging, and concurrency, but the reason→act→observe core is unchanged.
foundations.performanceImpact: Each loop iteration is a full model round-trip, so latency scales with the number of steps, not with tool speed. Tight tool descriptions and a low step cap reduce wasted turns; batching independent tool calls in one turn (covered later) cuts round-trips; a temperature of 0 makes the trajectory reproducible for debugging.
commonUseCases: Understanding what an agent framework does internally
Building a minimal agent without a heavyweight dependency
Debugging a stuck or runaway agent loop
Prototyping tool use before committing to a framework

commonMisconceptions.myth: The framework runs the loop, so I never need to understand it.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The framework runs *a* loop, and its defaults (step caps, error handling, message shape) leak into every bug you hit. Knowing the raw loop is what lets you diagnose those bugs.

commonMisconceptions.myth: The model keeps its own memory between calls.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The model is stateless. The only memory is the message list you resend on every call — forget to append a tool result and the model has literally never seen it.

commonMisconceptions.myth: The loop stops when the task is done.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The loop stops when the model returns no tool calls, which is a proxy for 'done'. Without a hard step cap alongside it, a confused model can loop forever.

codeLab.title: Build the agent loop from scratch
codeLab.instructions: Implement run_agent(client, goal, registry, max_steps=6) -> str. It must: (1) start a messages list with the user goal; (2) loop up to max_steps, calling client.chat(messages) each iteration; (3) if the response has no tool_calls, return its content (the stop condition); (4) otherwise, for each tool call, look the function up in `registry` by name, call it with **call['args'], and append a tool-result message with keys role='tool', tool_call_id set to the call's id, and content set to str(result); (5) raise RuntimeError if the step cap is exhausted without a final answer. The provided client and registry drive the harness.

starter.code:
def run_agent(client, goal, registry, max_steps=6):
    # TODO: build messages, loop, dispatch tools via registry,
    # append tool-result messages, honor the stop condition + step cap.
    ...

solution.code:
def run_agent(client, goal, registry, max_steps=6):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": goal}]
    for _ in range(max_steps):
        resp = client.chat(messages)                 # reason
        if not resp.tool_calls:                       # stop condition
            return resp.content
        for call in resp.tool_calls:                  # act
            fn = registry[call["name"]]               # dispatch by name
            result = fn(**call["args"])
            messages.append({                          # observe
                "role": "tool",
                "tool_call_id": call["id"],
                "content": str(result),
            })
    raise RuntimeError("agent hit step cap without finishing")

hints: The stop condition is simply 'the response has no tool_calls' — return resp.content then.
Dispatch is registry[call['name']] then call the result with **call['args'].
Each tool result becomes a message with role 'tool', the matching tool_call_id, and content as a string.

debuggingLab.title: The loop never terminates — and forgets the observation
debuggingLab.scenario: Your first hand-rolled agent hangs and eventually crashes on cost limits. It runs a tool over and over with the same arguments and never reaches a final answer. On inspection, two things are wrong: the loop has no step cap, and the tool result is computed but never appended to the messages, so the model re-requests the same tool forever because it never sees the observation.

buggyCode.code:
def run_agent(client, goal, registry):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": goal}]
    while True:                          # no step cap: can loop forever
        resp = client.chat(messages)
        if not resp.tool_calls:
            return resp.content
        for call in resp.tool_calls:
            result = registry[call["name"]](**call["args"])
            # BUG: result is computed but never appended!
            # the model never sees the observation, so it asks again
    # unreachable

debuggingLab.diagnosis: Two compounding bugs. First, `while True` has no upper bound, so if the model keeps requesting tools the loop runs until it hits an external cost or time limit. Second, and the real root cause, the tool result is computed but never appended to `messages`. Because the model is stateless and its only memory is the message list, it never observes the result, so on the next turn it sees the exact same history and re-requests the identical tool — an infinite loop by construction.

fix.code:
def run_agent(client, goal, registry, max_steps=8):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": goal}]
    for step in range(max_steps):              # hard cap backstop
        resp = client.chat(messages)
        if not resp.tool_calls:
            return resp.content
        # record the assistant's tool request so history stays coherent
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "tool_calls": resp.tool_calls})
        for call in resp.tool_calls:
            result = registry[call["name"]](**call["args"])
            messages.append({                   # FIX: feed the observation back
                "role": "tool",
                "tool_call_id": call["id"],
                "content": str(result),
            })
    raise RuntimeError("agent hit step cap without finishing")

debuggingLab.lesson: The message list is the agent's entire memory. If you compute a tool result but do not append it, the model literally never learns anything happened and will repeat itself. Always append the observation keyed by the tool_call_id, and always guard the loop with a hard step cap so that even a confused model or a bug in your dispatch can never run forever.
debuggingLab.expectedOutput: agent hit step cap without finishing

productionDeepDive.architecture: Structure the agent as three separable layers: a thin provider adapter that normalizes any vendor's response into a common {content, tool_calls} shape; a stateless registry mapping tool names to callables (plus their JSON Schemas); and a driver loop that owns message accumulation, dispatch, and termination. Keeping these separate means you can swap providers, add tools, or change the stop policy independently. The driver should treat messages as an append-only log and never mutate prior entries, which makes runs replayable from the transcript.
productionDeepDive.performance: Latency is dominated by the number of model round-trips, not tool execution, because each loop turn is a full generation. Cut turns by writing crisp tool descriptions (so the model picks the right tool first try), enabling parallel tool calls for independent actions, and keeping the step cap tight. Use temperature 0 for reproducibility, and cache the immutable system prompt and tool-schema prefix with provider prompt caching so repeated calls pay input tokens once.
productionDeepDive.reliability: Wrap every tool call in try/except and feed the error text back as the tool result rather than crashing the loop, so the model can recover or reroute. Bound the loop with both a step cap and a token/time budget, and treat cap exhaustion as a first-class, routed failure (fallback model, human handoff, or safe default) instead of an unhandled exception. Make dispatch tolerant of an unknown tool name by returning a clear error observation.
productionDeepDive.observability: Log every turn as a structured record: step index, the model's tool_calls, each tool's arguments, latency, and result (or error). Emit metrics for steps-per-task, tool error rate, and cap-exhaustion rate, broken down by tool and model version. Because the transcript is the full state, persisting the message list per run gives you a reproducible trace for any failure without extra instrumentation.
productionDeepDive.security: Tool arguments come from an untrusted model, so validate them at the registry boundary before execution — enforce enums, length limits, and allow-lists, and never pass model output to eval, shell, or SQL without parameterization. Scope each tool's real-world authority narrowly (least privilege), require human approval for irreversible actions, and strip secrets from anything you log since transcripts capture arguments verbatim.
productionDeepDive.cost: Cost tracks total tokens across all turns, which grows with both step count and the ever-lengthening message history resent each turn. Levers: minimize steps (good tools, parallel calls), summarize or truncate old turns when history gets long, cache the fixed schema/system prefix, and set a low temperature and tight step cap so runaway trajectories can't accumulate expensive turns.

caseStudies.problem: Their hand-rolled coding agent occasionally ran for dozens of turns and blew the per-task budget; investigation showed a subset of tasks where a flaky file-read tool raised, the exception was swallowed, no observation was appended, and the model re-requested the same read indefinitely.
caseStudies.solution: They added a hard step cap plus a token budget, wrapped each tool call so exceptions became a plain-text error observation fed back to the model, appended the assistant tool-call message so history stayed coherent, and emitted per-turn structured logs with steps-per-task and tool-error metrics.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: The error-as-observation approach occasionally lets the model retry a genuinely broken tool a couple of times before the cap fires, spending a few extra calls; in exchange runaway loops disappeared and every failure became a logged, bounded, reproducible event.
caseStudies.lessons: A stateless model plus a swallowed error equals an infinite loop. Always feed observations (including errors) back, always cap the loop two ways (steps and budget), and always log the transcript so a runaway is diagnosable in minutes.

checkpoints.prompt: What signals the agent loop to stop naturally?
options: The model returns content and no tool calls
The message list exceeds a size limit
checkpoints.explanation: The natural stop is when the model responds with final content and requests no further tools. A hard step cap is added alongside it as a backstop, but the done-signal is 'no tool_calls'.

checkpoints.prompt: This loop runs the tool but the agent still repeats it forever. Why?
options: The result is never appended to messages, so the stateless model never sees the observation and re-asks
registry should be a list, not a dict
checkpoints.explanation: The model is stateless; its only memory is the message list. The tool result is computed but never appended, so the next turn's history is identical and the model requests the same tool again — an infinite loop. Append a tool-result message keyed by call id.

checkpoints.prompt: Given this scripted client, what does run_agent print?
checkpoints.code:
def double(n): return n * 2
REG = {"double": double}
script = [
    {"content": None, "tool_calls": [{"id": "1", "name": "double", "args": {"n": 5}}]},
    {"content": "result is 10", "tool_calls": []},
]
# run_agent dispatches, appends the observation, then loops
print(run_agent(ScriptedClient(script), "double 5", REG))
checkpoints.explanation: Turn one requests double(5); the loop runs it and appends the observation. Turn two returns final content with no tool calls, so the loop returns 'result is 10'.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the tool-result message so the observation is linked to the right call.
checkpoints.explanation: The tool result must be keyed by the originating call's id so the model can match this observation to the specific request it made — essential when several tools are called in one turn.

theory.question: Walk through the agent loop from scratch — what are its parts and how do they fit together?
theory.directAnswer: The loop has four parts: a message list that is the agent's whole memory, a client call that lets the model reason, a tool registry that dispatches the model's chosen tool to a real function, and a stop condition. Each iteration calls the model, and if it requests tools you run them via the registry, append their results (observations) to the messages, and loop; when the model returns content with no tool calls you stop, guarded by a hard step cap.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An iterative reason→act→observe procedure that wraps a stateless LLM so it can take multiple tool-using steps toward a goal.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: The model cannot execute anything or remember across calls; the loop supplies the execution (via the registry), the memory (via the growing message list), and the control (via the stop condition).
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Start messages with the user goal; each turn call client.chat(messages, tools); if there are no tool_calls, return the content; otherwise dispatch each call through registry[name](**args), append a tool-result message keyed by the call id, and repeat until a natural stop or a step-cap backstop fires.

theory.whyImportant: Frameworks hide this loop, but its defaults leak into every agent bug; being able to write it by hand is the literacy needed to debug or build any agent system.
theory.realWorldExample: A coding assistant starts with 'fix the failing test', requests read_file, observes the source, requests run_tests, observes the failure, then returns a final patched-file answer — the same four-part loop with file tools.

followUps.question: Where is the agent's memory stored?
followUps.answer: Entirely in the message list you resend each call; the model itself is stateless, so an un-appended tool result is invisible to it.

followUps.question: Why have both a natural stop and a step cap?
followUps.answer: The natural stop ('no tool calls') is the intended exit, but a confused model or a dispatch bug can loop forever, so the step cap is a mandatory safety backstop.

theory.question: Why is the tool registry kept separate from the loop, and what does it buy you?
theory.directAnswer: The registry is a dict mapping tool names to callables, decoupled from the driver loop. This separation means the loop dispatches generically by name without hard-coding any tool, so adding a capability is just registering one more function, and swapping or validating tools happens in one place — the registry boundary — rather than scattered through the loop.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A lookup table (name → function) that the loop consults to turn the model's textual tool name into an actual Python call.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: The model can only emit a tool name and arguments as data; something must map that name to executable code, and centralizing it keeps the loop generic.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The loop reads call.name, looks up registry[call.name], and invokes it with **call.args; validation, error wrapping, and least-privilege scoping all live at this single boundary.

theory.whyImportant: Centralizing dispatch is what makes an agent extensible and secure: new tools plug in without touching the loop, and argument validation guards one choke point instead of many.
theory.realWorldExample: Adding a new 'refund_order' capability to a support agent means writing the function and adding one registry entry; the loop, logging, and validation all keep working unchanged.

followUps.question: What happens if the model requests a name not in the registry?
followUps.answer: Dispatch should return a clear error observation (e.g. 'unknown tool: foo') fed back to the model rather than raising, so the loop can recover.

followUps.question: Where do you validate tool arguments?
followUps.answer: At the registry boundary before calling the function — enforce enums, lengths, and allow-lists there since arguments come from untrusted model output.

scenario.question: Your hand-rolled agent occasionally runs for 40+ turns and blows the budget on a subset of tasks. How do you diagnose and fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: First bound the blast radius with a hard step cap and a token/time budget so runaways can't recur. Then read the persisted transcripts for the offending tasks to find the repeating pattern — usually the same tool re-requested with identical arguments, which means the observation isn't reaching the model (a swallowed tool exception or an un-appended result). Fix by wrapping tool calls so errors become plain-text observations, ensuring every result is appended keyed by call id, and adding metrics for steps-per-task and tool-error rate.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A runaway-loop reliability problem where the agent fails to progress and accumulates cost across turns.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A stateless model plus a missing observation (from a swallowed error or a forgotten append) makes each turn's history identical, so the model repeats itself indefinitely; without a cap the loop never breaks.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Persist transcripts, group runaway tasks, and inspect the message list — identical consecutive tool requests point to a missing observation; add the cap and budget as backstops, convert exceptions to error observations, and instrument per-turn metrics to catch regressions.

scenario.whyImportant: It shows the metrics-and-transcript-driven approach and the core insight that missing observations, not the model, cause most runaway loops.
scenario.realWorldExample: A flaky file-read tool raised, the exception was swallowed, no observation was appended, and the model re-requested the read every turn until an external cost limit killed it; feeding the error back as an observation plus a step cap fixed it.

followUps.question: Why not just lower the step cap and move on?
followUps.answer: A low cap hides the symptom but the task still fails; you must fix the missing observation so the model can actually progress, with the cap as a backstop.

followUps.question: How do you catch a recurrence early?
followUps.answer: Alert on steps-per-task and cap-exhaustion rate per tool and model version so a regression (e.g. a newly flaky tool) is visible before it inflates the bill.

coding.question: Implement a minimal agent loop: given a client, a goal, and a tool registry, run reason→act→observe until the model stops, with a step-cap backstop.
coding.thoughtProcess: The message list is the only state, so I seed it with the goal and resend it every turn. Each turn I call the client; if there are no tool calls I return the content (the natural stop). Otherwise I dispatch each call through the registry, append a tool-result message keyed by the call id so the observation reaches the model, and loop. A for-range over max_steps guarantees termination, and exhausting it raises so a runaway is a handled failure, not a hang.
lineByLine: messages seeds the only state with the user goal and is resent every turn.
The for-range over max_steps guarantees the loop cannot run forever.
client.chat is the reason phase; no tool_calls means the model answered, so we return its content.
Dispatch looks up the callable by name and invokes it with the model's arguments.
Unknown tools and tool exceptions become plain-text error observations instead of crashing the loop.
Each result is appended as a tool message keyed by call id so the stateless model observes it.
Exhausting the step cap raises a handled RuntimeError rather than hanging.
coding.timeComplexity: O(steps) model round-trips; per turn O(t) in the number of tool calls t.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(steps) growth of the message list, since history is append-only.

followUps.question: How would you add parallel tool execution?
followUps.answer: When resp.tool_calls has several independent calls, run them concurrently (threads or asyncio) and append results preserving each call id — covered in the parallel-tool-calls topic.

followUps.question: How do you keep history from growing unbounded on long tasks?
followUps.answer: Summarize or drop older turns once the message list crosses a token threshold, keeping the goal and recent observations.

keyTakeaways: An agent is a loop you own: reason (call the model) → act (run the requested tool via a registry) → observe (append the result) → repeat.
The message list is the agent's entire memory; the model is stateless, so an un-appended tool result is invisible to it.
A tool registry (name → callable) keeps dispatch generic and centralizes validation, so adding a tool is one line.
Stop on the natural signal (no tool calls) but always guard with a hard step cap so a confused model can't loop forever.
In production, wrap tools so errors become observations, log the transcript, bound with steps + budget, and validate arguments at the registry boundary.
